claim: Mushroom bodies (MB) of adult Drosophila have a core of thousands of Kenyon neurons.
source: Mushroom bodies (MB) of adult Drosophila have a core of thousands of Kenyon neurons; axons of the early-born g class form a medial lobe and those from later-born α'β' and αβ classes form both medial and vertical lobes.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the structure of adult Drosophila mushroom bodies.

claim: Axons of the early-born γ class Kenyon neurons form a medial lobe.
source: Mushroom bodies (MB) of adult Drosophila have a core of thousands of Kenyon neurons; axons of the early-born g class form a medial lobe and those from later-born α'β' and αβ classes form both medial and vertical lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of γ class Kenyon neurons.

claim: Axons from later-born α'β' and αβ classes of Kenyon neurons form both medial and vertical lobes.
source: Mushroom bodies (MB) of adult Drosophila have a core of thousands of Kenyon neurons; axons of the early-born g class form a medial lobe and those from later-born α'β' and αβ classes form both medial and vertical lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the axonal projections of later-born Kenyon cell classes.

claim: The larva hatches with only γ neurons.
source: The larva, however, hatches with only γ neurons and forms a vertical lobe 'facsimile' using larval-specific axon branches from its γ neurons.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract describing the larval MB composition.

claim: The larva forms a vertical lobe 'facsimile' using larval-specific axon branches from its γ neurons.
source: The larva, however, hatches with only γ neurons and forms a vertical lobe 'facsimile' using larval-specific axon branches from its γ neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a larval-specific adaptation.

claim: MB input (MBINs) and output (MBONs) neurons divide the Kenyon neuron lobes into discrete computational compartments.
source: MB input (MBINs) and output (MBONs) neurons divide the Kenyon neuron lobes into discrete computational compartments.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the functional organization of the MB.

claim: The larva has 10 MB compartments.
source: The larva has 10 such compartments while the adult has 16.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The adult has 16 MB compartments.
source: The larva has 10 such compartments while the adult has 16.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The fates of 28 of the 32 MBONs and MBINs that define the 10 larval compartments were determined.
source: We determined the fates of 28 of the 32 MBONs and MBINs that define the 10 larval compartments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: Seven larval compartments are subsequently incorporated into the adult MB.
source: Seven compartments are subsequently incorporated into the adult MB; four of their MBINs die, while 12 MBINs/MBONs remodel to function in adult compartments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the fate mapping study.

claim: Four MBINs from compartments incorporated into the adult MB die.
source: Seven compartments are subsequently incorporated into the adult MB; four of their MBINs die, while 12 MBINs/MBONs remodel to function in adult compartments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the fate mapping study.

claim: 12 MBINs/MBONs remodel to function in adult compartments.
source: Seven compartments are subsequently incorporated into the adult MB; four of their MBINs die, while 12 MBINs/MBONs remodel to function in adult compartments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the fate mapping study.

claim: Three larval compartments are larval specific.
source: The remaining three compartments are larval specific.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing compartments not incorporated into the adult MB.

claim: At metamorphosis, MBINs/MBONs from larval-specific compartments trans-differentiate, leaving the MB for other adult brain circuits.
source: At metamorphosis their MBIN/MBONs trans-differentiate, leaving the MB for other adult brain circuits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the fate of neurons from larval-specific compartments.

claim: The adult vertical lobes are made de novo using MBONs/MBINs recruited from pools of adult-specific neurons.
source: The adult vertical lobes are made de novo using MBONs/MBINs recruited from pools of adult-specific neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about adult vertical lobe formation.

claim: No larval MBIN-MBON connections are maintained through metamorphosis.
source: The combination of cell death, compartment shifting, trans-differentiation, and recruitment of new neurons result in no larval MBIN-MBON connections being maintained through metamorphosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: There is no anatomical substrate for a memory trace persisting from larva to adult at the level of MBIN-MBON connections.
source: At this simple level, then, we find no anatomical substrate for a memory trace persisting from larva to adult.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the finding that no MBIN-MBON connections persist.

claim: The adult phenotype of trans-differentiating neurons represents their evolutionarily ancestral phenotype.
source: The adult phenotype of the trans-differentiating neurons represents their evolutionarily ancestral phenotype while their larval phenotype is a derived adaptation for the larval stage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the trans-differentiation findings.

claim: The larval phenotype of trans-differentiating neurons is a derived adaptation for the larval stage.
source: The adult phenotype of the trans-differentiating neurons represents their evolutionarily ancestral phenotype while their larval phenotype is a derived adaptation for the larval stage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the trans-differentiation findings.

claim: Trans-differentiating neurons arise primarily within lineages that also produce permanent MBINs and MBONs.
source: These cells arise primarily within lineages that also produce permanent MBINs and MBONs, suggesting that larval specifying factors may allow information related to birth-order or sibling identity to be interpreted in a modified manner in the larva to allow these neurons to acquire larval phenotypic modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the lineage origins of trans-differentiating neurons.

claim: Larval specifying factors may allow information related to birth-order or sibling identity to be interpreted in a modified manner in the larva.
source: These cells arise primarily within lineages that also produce permanent MBINs and MBONs, suggesting that larval specifying factors may allow information related to birth-order or sibling identity to be interpreted in a modified manner in the larva to allow these neurons to acquire larval phenotypic modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculation about the mechanism of larval phenotype acquisition.

claim: The loss of larval specifying factors at metamorphosis allows trans-differentiating neurons to revert to their ancestral functions in the adult.
source: The loss of such factors at metamorphosis then allows these neurons to revert to their ancestral functions in the adult.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculation about the mechanism of trans-differentiation.

claim: Direct developing insects like crickets and grasshoppers produce a species-typical body form during embryogenesis.
source: Direct developing insects like crickets and grasshoppers produce a species-typical body form during embryogenesis and hatch as a miniature version of the adult but lack wings and genitalia.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as background information about direct developing insects.

claim: Direct developing insects hatch as a miniature version of the adult but lack wings and genitalia.
source: Direct developing insects like crickets and grasshoppers produce a species-typical body form during embryogenesis and hatch as a miniature version of the adult but lack wings and genitalia.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as background information about direct developing insects.

claim: Holometabolous insects have modified their embryogenesis to produce a simplified larval body instead.
source: Holometabolous insects, which have complete metamorphosis, have modified their embryogenesis to produce a simplified larval body instead (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as background information about holometabolous insects.

claim: In the larval body, embryonic fields are only partially patterned, with the patterned portion making the larval structure and the remainder preserved through larval growth to become imaginal discs or primordia.
source: In the larval body, embryonic fields, which had been fully utilized to generate their adult-like structures, are only partially patterned, with the patterned portion making the larval structure and the remainder preserved through larval growth to become imaginal discs or primordia.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the developmental strategy of holometabolous insects.

claim: The imaginal primordia, along with some larval cells, combine to construct the species-typical body form at metamorphosis.
source: The imaginal primordia, along with some larval cells, combine to construct the species-typical body form at metamorphosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing how the adult body is formed in holometabolous insects.

claim: Direct development results in a hatchling possessing an essentially mature, but miniature brain, which is used for both the nymphal and adult stages.
source: Direct development also results in a hatchling possessing an essentially mature, but miniature brain, which is used for both the nymphal and adult stages (reviews by Kutsch and Heckmann, 1995; Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The evolution of the larva altered brain development to make a modified, simpler brain appropriate for the sensory and motor demands of the larva.
source: The evolution of the larva, though, altered brain development to make a modified, simpler brain appropriate for the sensory and motor demands of the larva.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the impact of larval evolution on brain development.

claim: The larval brain is not discarded at the end of larval growth and a new one made from scratch.
source: This larval brain, though, is not discarded at the end of larval growth and a new one made from scratch.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the fate of the larval brain.

claim: Most larval neurons persist through metamorphosis.
source: Most larval neurons persist and some, like the interneurons mediating backwards locomotion, have similar functions in both larva and adult (Lee and Doe, 2021), but, as we show in this paper, the maintenance of neuronal function from larva to adult is not always the case.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Some larval neurons, like the interneurons mediating backwards locomotion, have similar functions in both larva and adult.
source: Most larval neurons persist and some, like the interneurons mediating backwards locomotion, have similar functions in both larva and adult (Lee and Doe, 2021), but, as we show in this paper, the maintenance of neuronal function from larva to adult is not always the case.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: At metamorphosis, recycled larval cells are combined with adult-specific neurons to make the nervous system of the adult.
source: At metamorphosis, recycled larval cells are combined with adult-specific neurons to make the nervous system of the adult (Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: One key embryonic change involved neurogenesis.
source: One key embryonic change involved neurogenesis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a key change associated with larval evolution.

claim: The central brain and ventral nerve cord (VNC) of insects arise from a fixed number of neuronal stem cells (neuroblasts [NBs]), with about 100 per brain hemisphere.
source: The central brain and ventral nerve cord (VNC) of insects arise from a fixed number of neuronal stem cells (neuroblasts [NBs]), with about 100 per brain hemisphere (Urbach and Technau, 2003) and about 30 per segmental hemineuropil (Thomas et al., 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: There are about 30 neuroblasts per segmental hemineuropil in the VNC.
source: The central brain and ventral nerve cord (VNC) of insects arise from a fixed number of neuronal stem cells (neuroblasts [NBs]), with about 100 per brain hemisphere (Urbach and Technau, 2003) and about 30 per segmental hemineuropil (Thomas et al., 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Each neuroblast makes a characteristic set of neurons in a defined temporal order.
source: Each NB makes a characteristic set of neurons in a defined temporal order (Kohwi and Doe, 2013; Doe, 2017; Miyares and Lee, 2019; Rossi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The sets of NBs in the brain and VNC are highly conserved and were established well before the evolution of the larva and complete metamorphosis.
source: The sets of NBs in the brain and VNC, though, are highly conserved and were established well before the evolution of the larva and complete metamorphosis (Thomas et al., 1984; Truman and Ball, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: These conserved sets of NBs produce the neurons for both the larval and adult CNS.
source: Moreover, these conserved sets of NBs produce the neurons for both the larval and adult CNS (Prokop and Technau, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The duration of embryonic neurogenesis differs in direct developing and holometabolous insects.
source: The duration of embryonic neurogenesis, however, differs in the two groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a key difference between the two developmental strategies.

claim: Insects with direct development produce all the neurons of the central brain and VNC during embryogenesis.
source: Insects with direct development, like grasshoppers, produce all the neurons of the central brain and VNC during embryogenesis (Shepherd and Bate, 1990) and the hatchling possesses all the neurons of the adult (except for expansion of the Kenyon cell population, e.g., Malaterre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The hatchling of direct developing insects possesses all the neurons of the adult (except for expansion of the Kenyon cell population).
source: Insects with direct development, like grasshoppers, produce all the neurons of the central brain and VNC during embryogenesis (Shepherd and Bate, 1990) and the hatchling possesses all the neurons of the adult (except for expansion of the Kenyon cell population, e.g., Malaterre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In insects with complete metamorphosis, selection for the rapid formation of a larval stage required a premature arrest of neurogenesis, resulting in many fewer neurons for the larval brain.
source: In insects with complete metamorphosis, by contrast, selection for the rapid formation of a larval stage required a premature arrest of neurogenesis, resulting in many fewer neurons for the larval brain (Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In Drosophila, most brain and thoracic NBs produce only 10–15% of their respective progeny by hatching.
source: In Drosophila, for example, most brain and thoracic NBs produce only 10–15% of their respective progeny by hatching and the remainder are made during a second neurogenic period late in larval growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an example of the premature arrest of neurogenesis in holometabolous insects.

claim: The remainder of neuroblast progeny in Drosophila are made during a second neurogenic period late in larval growth.
source: In Drosophila, for example, most brain and thoracic NBs produce only 10–15% of their respective progeny by hatching and the remainder are made during a second neurogenic period late in larval growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the timing of neurogenesis in Drosophila.

claim: The hatchlings of direct developing insects have brain circuits that include neurons generated during early, intermediate, and late phases of their neuroblasts' lineages.
source: Since essentially all their neurons are born during embryogenesis, the hatchlings of direct developing insects have brain circuits that include neurons generated during early, intermediate, and late phases of their neuroblasts' lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a consequence of complete embryonic neurogenesis.

claim: The larvae of metamorphic insects have fewer neurons to make their brain, and these neurons include only those with early-born fates.
source: The larvae of metamorphic insects, by contrast, not only have fewer neurons to make their brain, but these neurons include only those with early-born fates.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a consequence of premature arrest of neurogenesis.

claim: A second key change involves the phenotypes of the neurons that are made during embryogenesis.
source: A second key change involves the phenotypes of the neurons that are made during embryogenesis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as another key change associated with larval evolution.

claim: The neurons of direct developing insects acquire their mature phenotype by the time of hatching and their anatomy and connections change very little through nymphal growth and adulthood.
source: The neurons of direct developing insects acquire their mature phenotype by the time of hatching and their anatomy and connections change very little through nymphal growth and adulthood (Kutsch and Heckmann, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In holometabolous insects, the form and function of many larval neurons are radically different from their adult form and function.
source: By contrast, in holometabolous insects, the form and function of many larval neurons are radically different from their adult form and function (e.g., Truman and Reiss, 1976; Levine and Truman, 1985; Roy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: At metamorphosis, larval neurons lose their larval specializations and finally acquire their mature, adult phenotypes.
source: At metamorphosis, they lose their larval specializations and finally acquire their mature, adult phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the metamorphic transformation of larval neurons.

claim: In both larval and adult stages, the MBs associate odors with either rewards or punishments and adjust the animal's future behavior accordingly.
source: In both stages, the MBs associate odors with either rewards or punishments and adjust the animal's future behavior accordingly (Cognigni et al., 2018; Thum and Gerber, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim about MB function.

claim: The circuitry of the MB is known at the EM level for both the larva and adult.
source: The circuitry of the MB is known at the EM level for both the larva (Eichler et al., 2017) and adult (Zheng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The core of the MB is a set of hundreds (larva) to thousands (adult) of small neurons called Kenyon cells.
source: The core of the MB is a set of hundreds (larva) to thousands (adult) of small neurons called Kenyon cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Kenyon cell dendrites project into calyx neuropil, which receives primarily olfactory input via antennal lobe projection neurons.
source: Their dendrites project into calyx neuropil, which receives primarily olfactory input via antennal lobe projection neurons, and into accessory calyx neuropils that receive visual and thermal information (Li et al., 2020; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Kenyon cell dendrites project into accessory calyx neuropils that receive visual and thermal information.
source: Their dendrites project into calyx neuropil, which receives primarily olfactory input via antennal lobe projection neurons, and into accessory calyx neuropils that receive visual and thermal information (Li et al., 2020; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The bundled axons of the Kenyon cells extend down the peduncle and into the vertical and medial lobes.
source: The bundled axons of the Kenyon cells extend down the peduncle and into the vertical and medial lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing Kenyon cell anatomy.

claim: The mature, adult MB has three major classes of Kenyon cells: the γ neurons made during embryogenesis and early larval life, the α'β' cells generated late in larval life, and the αβ neurons born through early and mid-metamorphosis.
source: The mature, adult MB has three major classes of Kenyon cells: the γ neurons made during embryogenesis and early larval life, the α'β' cells generated late in larval life, and the αβneurons born through early and mid-metamorphosis (Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Kenyon cell axons form three medial lobes (γ, β', β) and two vertical lobes (α, α').
source: There is considerable complexity within each of these major Kenyon cell classes (Eichler et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020), but overall, their axons form three medial lobes (γ, β', β) and two vertical lobes (α, α') (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The MB of the larva contains only modified γ Kenyon cells whose axons form a vertical and a medial lobe.
source: Unlike the adult, the MB of the larva contains only modified γ Kenyon cells whose axons form a vertical and a medial lobe (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: MBINs and MBONs that innervate the peduncle and lobes divide the lobes into non-overlapping compartments.
source: The MB receives flows of sensory information through projection neurons to the calyx, but our study focused on the sets of MB input neurons (MBINs) and output neurons (MBONs) that innervate the peduncle and lobes (Figure 2A and B). In both larvae and adults, these neurons divide the lobes into non-overlapping compartments (Figure 2C) that have a common microcircuit motif (Figure 2D; Eichler et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Each MB compartment is defined by the axonal tuft of an aminergic input cell that synapses onto Kenyon cell axons and onto a dedicated MBON(s).
source: Each compartment is defined by the axonal tuft of an aminergic input cell that synapses onto Kenyon cell axons and onto a dedicated MBON(s).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the microcircuit structure of MB compartments.

claim: The Kenyon cell axons synapse onto each other and the MBONs but also feed back onto the MBINs.
source: The Kenyon cell axons synapse onto each other and the MBONs but also feed back onto the MBINs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: The majority of the MBINs are dopaminergic neurons (DANs) but a few are octopaminergic neurons (OANs).
source: The majority of the MBINs are dopaminergic neurons (DANs) but a few are octopaminergic neurons (OANs).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the neurotransmitter types of MBINs.

claim: Most DANs come from two clusters, the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster, which primarily encodes reward, and the protocerebral posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster, which mainly encodes punishment.
source: Most DANs come from two clusters, the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster, which primarily encodes reward, and the protocerebral posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster, which mainly encodes punishment (Saumweber et al., 2018; Cognigni et al., 2018; Eichler et al., 2017; Eschbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Depending on their compartment, the MBONs are cholinergic, GABAergic, or glutaminergic.
source: Depending on their compartment, the MBONs are cholinergic, GABAergic, or glutaminergic.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the neurotransmitter types of MBONs.

claim: Stimulation of the MBONs from PPL1-supplied compartments generally evokes approach behavior.
source: Interestingly, stimulation of the MBONs from PPL1-supplied compartments generally evokes approach behavior while stimulation of those from PAM supplied compartments evokes avoidance (Owald et al., 2015; Cognigni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Stimulation of MBONs from PAM supplied compartments evokes avoidance.
source: Interestingly, stimulation of the MBONs from PPL1-supplied compartments generally evokes approach behavior while stimulation of those from PAM supplied compartments evokes avoidance (Owald et al., 2015; Cognigni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Pairing punishment with a particular odor reduces the drive on MBONs that promote attraction.
source: Consequently, pairing punishment with a particular odor reduces the drive on MBONs that promote attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a consequence of the MB circuit organization.

claim: Behavior is guided by a balance of avoidance versus attractive influences and the inhibition of neurons mediating one behavior then favors the opposite behavioral state.
source: Behavior is therefore guided by a balance of avoidance versus attractive influences and the inhibition of neurons mediating one behavior then favors the opposite behavioral state (Thum and Gerber, 2019; Cognigni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The functions of some compartments are complex because of extensive interconnections amongst MBONs and feedback from MBONs back to various MBINs.
source: The functions of some compartments, though, are complex because of extensive interconnections amongst MBONs and feedback from MBONs back to various MBINs (e.g., Eschbach et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The larval MB has 10 compartments plus the calyx.
source: The larval MB has 10 compartments plus the calyx (Saumweber et al., 2018; Eichler et al., 2017), while the adult has 16 (Aso et al., 2014; Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The larval structure lacks the α'β' and αβ neurons that form the adult system's vertical lobes.
source: The larval structure lacks the α'β' and αβ neurons that form the adult system's vertical lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing differences between larval and adult MB.

claim: The larval γ neurons have larval-specific vertical axon branches that form the core of a larval vertical lobe.
source: The larval γ neurons, though, have larval-specific vertical axon branches that form the core of a larval vertical lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the larval-specific anatomy of γ neurons.

claim: The metamorphic fates of about 80% of the MBINs and MBONs that establish the 10 larval compartments were determined.
source: We have focused on the MBINs and MBONs that establish the 10 larval compartments (Eichler et al., 2017; Saumweber et al., 2018). We have determined the metamorphic fates of about 80% of these neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: Depending on the fate of their compartment, some larval neurons remain with the MB, others reprogram to join other adult circuits, and still others die.
source: Depending on the fate of their compartment, some larval neurons remain with the MB, others reprogram to join other adult circuits, and still others die.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction summarizing the findings.

claim: The diverse fates of the larval MB neurons plus the addition of new, adult-specific MBINs and MBONs to the compartments result in no MBIN-MBON pairings that survive from larva to adult.
source: The persistence of MBON to MBIN connections would have been the simplest way that a larval memory trace could be carried through metamorphosis. However, we find that the diverse fates of the larval MB neurons plus the addition of new, adult-specific MBINs and MBONs to the compartments result in no MBIN-MBON pairings that survive from larva to adult.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: Armstrong et al., 1998 used a set of enhancer-trap lines to follow subsets of extrinsic and intrinsic MB neurons through metamorphosis.
source: Armstrong et al., 1998 used a set of enhancer-trap lines to follow subsets of extrinsic and intrinsic MB neurons through metamorphosis and showed that some of the medial lobe neurons functioned in both the larval and adult structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to prior work.

claim: Armstrong et al., 1998 showed that some of the medial lobe neurons functioned in both the larval and adult structures.
source: Armstrong et al., 1998 used a set of enhancer-trap lines to follow subsets of extrinsic and intrinsic MB neurons through metamorphosis and showed that some of the medial lobe neurons functioned in both the larval and adult structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to prior work.

claim: The fates of 28 of the 32 classes of unicompartmental MBINs and MBONs could be determined.
source: We focused on the larval unicompartmental neurons that possess the well-defined dendritic or axonal 'tufts' that define compartments (Saumweber et al., 2018), and we could determine the fates of 28 of the 32 classes of such cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding of the study.

claim: Persisting neurons are classified as 'remodeling' if they continue as part of the MB circuitry after metamorphosis.
source: We have classified the persisting neurons as 'remodeling' if they continue as part of the MB circuitry after metamorphosis or as 'trans-differentiating' (see Veverytsa and Allan, 2013) if they retract from the MB system and function in other circuits of the adult brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section defining the classification scheme.

claim: Persisting neurons are classified as 'trans-differentiating' if they retract from the MB system and function in other circuits of the adult brain.
source: We have classified the persisting neurons as 'remodeling' if they continue as part of the MB circuitry after metamorphosis or as 'trans-differentiating' (see Veverytsa and Allan, 2013) if they retract from the MB system and function in other circuits of the adult brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section defining the classification scheme with a citation.

claim: The two designations of remodeling and trans-differentiating are likely the two extremes along a continuum of change.
source: These two designations, however, likely are the two extremes along a continuum of change.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the classification scheme.

claim: The fates of 13 of the remaining 14 larval MBINs were experimentally established.
source: We lacked suitable lines for the two octopaminergic neurons that innervate the calyx compartment (OAN-a1 and -a2). However, these cells have a very similar anatomy to the two adult OA-VUM2a neurons (Busch et al., 2009), leading us to conclude that they are the same neurons. We experimentally established the fates of 13 of the remaining 14 larval MBINs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding of the study.

claim: OAN-a1 and -a2 have a very similar anatomy to the two adult OA-VUM2a neurons.
source: We lacked suitable lines for the two octopaminergic neurons that innervate the calyx compartment (OAN-a1 and -a2). However, these cells have a very similar anatomy to the two adult OA-VUM2a neurons (Busch et al., 2009), leading us to conclude that they are the same neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: OAN-a1 and -a2 are the same neurons as the adult OA-VUM2a neurons.
source: We lacked suitable lines for the two octopaminergic neurons that innervate the calyx compartment (OAN-a1 and -a2). However, these cells have a very similar anatomy to the two adult OA-VUM2a neurons (Busch et al., 2009), leading us to conclude that they are the same neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on anatomical similarity.

claim: Larval MBINs either trans-differentiate, remodel, or degenerate.
source: These cells either trans-differentiate, remodel, or degenerate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section summarizing the fates of larval MBINs.

claim: Trans-differentiation was the fate of one MBIN innervating the LA compartment and all those innervating the vertical lobe compartments, UVL and IVL, and the intermediate peduncle (IP) compartment.
source: Trans-differentiation was the fate of one MBIN innervating the LA compartment and all those innervating the vertical lobe compartments, UVL and IVL, and the intermediate peduncle (IP) compartment (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: MBINs-b1 and -b2 withdraw from the larval intermediate peduncle and become sexually dimorphic neurons that innervate the adult optic lobes.
source: The most extreme change was evident for MBINs-b1 and -b2; they withdraw from the larval intermediate peduncle and become sexually dimorphic neurons that innervate the adult optic lobes (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: GFP expression typically persists through enough of the remodeling period to confirm a neuron's adult identity.

claim: The medial lobe MBINs (DAN-h1 to -k1) degenerate early in metamorphosis.
source: As expected from our failure to find the adult versions of the medial lobe MBINs (DAN-h1 to -k1) using the flip-switch method, we found that they degenerate early in metamorphosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The dendritic arbors of medial lobe MBINs collapsed by 8 hr after puparium formation (APF).

claim: The cell bodies of medial lobe MBINs were disrupted by 16 hr APF.
source: Their dendritic arbors collapsed by 8 hr after puparium formation (APF), the cell bodies were disrupted by 16 hr APF, and the neurons were reduced to scattered GFP-labeled debris by 24 hr APF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the time course of degeneration.

claim: The medial lobe MBINs were reduced to scattered GFP-labeled debris by 24 hr APF.
source: Their dendritic arbors collapsed by 8 hr after puparium formation (APF), the cell bodies were disrupted by 16 hr APF, and the neurons were reduced to scattered GFP-labeled debris by 24 hr APF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the time course of degeneration.

source: The latter form, with its single medially directed axon, is the same as seen in the γ neurons of nymphs and adults of the more basal, direct-developing insects, such as the cricket (Malaterre et al., 2002).

claim: Midline spiking interneurons were first described in grasshoppers.

claim: Midline spiking interneurons are found in both direct developing and metamorphic insects, indicating their involvement in leg function through insect evolution.
source: They were first described in grasshoppers (Siegler and Burrows, 1984) but they are found in both direct developing and metamorphic insects (Witten and Truman, 1998), indicating their involvement in leg function through insect evolution.
